title: Valongo Wharf, Rio de Janeiro
summary: Valongo Wharf was a stone landing place in Rio de Janeiro's harbour, begun in 1811, where enslaved Africans were brought ashore; UNESCO estimates up to 900,000 passed through. Later paving and a new wharf in 1843 covered it. It was rediscovered in 2011 and inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2017 as a site of conscience.

uncertainty.note: Construction began in 1811 (UNESCO); the Empress' Wharf was built over it in 1843 (UNESCO). The date the landing of enslaved Africans at the wharf ended is not stated on the opened pages.

as_recorded.value: for the landing of enslaved Africans reaching the South American continent from 1811 onwards

where.modern_name: Praca Jornal do Comercio, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil
where.historical_name: Cais do Valongo, harbour of Rio de Janeiro (Portuguese Brazil, later the Empire of Brazil)

importance.justification: Described by UNESCO as the most important physical trace of the arrival of enslaved Africans on the American continent.

audience_note: Concerns the landing place of enslaved Africans in the transatlantic slave trade; the entry describes the site and its significance without graphic detail.
